entry: Dutch navigator, cartographer, and [[Arctic]] explorer. Born on the island of Terschelling, Barentsz was a mapmaker who co-published an atlas of the Mediterranean with Petrus Plancius before devoting his career to finding a Northeast Passage to China. His first two voyages, in 1594 and 1595, were turned back by ice in the [[Kara Sea]] and near [[Novaya Zemlya]], although his crews met a [[Polar bear|polar bear]] and [[Walrus|walruses]]. On a third expedition, in 1596, the crew discovered Bear Island and Spitsbergen, but was trapped on Novaya Zemlya for almost a year. Barentsz died on the return voyage. The [[Barents Sea]] is named after him.

English jurist, judge, and Tory politician. Blackstone's lectures on English law, begun in 1753, were a success and were published as *An Analysis of the Laws of England* (1756). In 1759 he became the first Vinerian Professor of English Law at Oxford. His four-volume *Commentaries on the Laws of England*, first published from 1765, became the best-known description of the English [[Common law|common law]], and reprints appeared into the 1870s. He was elected a Tory member of Parliament for Hindon in 1761, and was appointed a justice of the Court of King's Bench in 1770, moving to the Court of Common Pleas that year. In the United States, the *Commentaries* influenced [[Alexander Hamilton]], [[John Adams]], and [[Abraham Lincoln]].

English poet, painter, and printmaker. Largely unrecognized during his lifetime, Blake is now regarded as a seminal figure in the poetry and visual art of the [[Romanticism|Romantic]] Age. Contemporaries considered him mad for his idiosyncratic views, but later critics praised the expressiveness of his work and its mystical undercurrents. He was hostile to the [[Church of England]] and to most organized religion, and was influenced by the French and American revolutions, though he later rejected many of his political beliefs. He maintained an amicable relationship with the political activist [[Thomas Paine]]. His wife, Catherine Boucher, worked as a printmaker and colorist on many of his books. Apart from three years in Felpham, he lived in London his entire life.

British statesman and four-time prime minister of the United Kingdom, from 1868 to 1894. Born in [[Liverpool]], Gladstone entered Parliament in 1832 as a Tory, served under [[Robert Peel]], and after 1846 joined the Peelite faction that merged into the Liberal Party. His first ministry disestablished the Church of Ireland and introduced the secret ballot. His Midlothian campaign of 1879–1880 is considered the first modern political campaign in Britain. His second ministry passed the Third Reform Act but ended in his resignation after public outrage over the death of General Gordon at Khartoum. His 1886 proposal for Irish home rule split the Liberal Party, and he resigned in 1894, aged 84, as the oldest prime minister ever. Historians often rank him among Britain's greatest prime ministers.

American novelist and short-story writer, best known for works set in the fictional Yoknapatawpha County, [[Mississippi]]. Faulkner was born in New Albany and raised in Oxford, Mississippi. He joined the Royal Canadian Air Force during [[World War I]] but did not see combat. His novels include *The Sound and the Fury* (1929), *As I Lay Dying* (1930), and *Light in August*. He also worked as a screenwriter on films by [[Howard Hawks]], including *To Have and Have Not* and *The Big Sleep*, the latter adapted from [[Raymond Chandler]]'s novel. Awarded the 1949 Nobel Prize in Literature, he is the only Mississippi-born Nobel laureate. Two of his works, *A Fable* and *The Reivers*, won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. He died of a heart attack a month after a fall from his horse.

American director, producer, and screenwriter of the [[New Hollywood]] movement. He is best known for *The French Connection* (1971), which won five [[Academy Awards]], including Best Picture and Best Director, and for the horror film *The Exorcist* (1973), which earned him another Best Director nomination. His other films include *The Boys in the Band* (1970), regarded as a milestone of queer cinema, and *Sorcerer* (1977). From 1998 he worked extensively as an opera director. His last feature, *The Caine Mutiny Court-Martial* (2023), was released two months after his death.

English physician, physicist, and natural philosopher. Gilbert rejected both Aristotelian philosophy and the scholastic method of university teaching. His book *De Magnete* (1600), based on experiments with a model Earth he called a terrella, concluded that the Earth is itself [[Magnetism|magnetic]], which explains why [[Compass|compasses]] point north. He was the first to argue that the Earth's center was iron. Studying the attraction of [[Amber|amber]] when rubbed, he coined the Neo-Latin term *electricus* ("like amber") and built the first electrical measuring instrument, the electroscope. A unit of magnetomotive force, the gilbert, was named in his honor and has since been superseded by the ampere-turn. He was elected president of the Royal College of Physicians in 1600 and was physician to [[Elizabeth I]] from 1601 until her death.

English physician, anatomist, and physiologist. Harvey was the first known physician to describe completely, and in detail, pulmonary and systemic circulation and the pumping of [[Blood|blood]] by the [[Heart|heart]]. Earlier writers, including Realdo Colombo and Michael Servetus, had anticipated some of his theories. He studied at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]] and then at the University of Padua, took his medical degree in 1602, and from 1609 was physician at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London for almost the rest of his life. His *Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus* (1628) used vivisection and quantitative measurement to show that blood flows in one direction, from arteries to veins, through a circuit driven by the heart, with one-way valves in the veins.

British [[X-ray]] crystallographer. Bragg was Elder Professor of Mathematics and Physics at the University of [[Adelaide]] from 1885, where he improved the teaching facilities by apprenticing himself to instrument makers. In 1896 he demonstrated X-rays to local doctors, following [[Wilhelm Röntgen|Röntgen]]'s discovery of them. His lifelong friendship with [[Ernest Rutherford]] began when Rutherford visited him in 1895. With his son Lawrence Bragg, he shared the 1915 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics "for their services in the analysis of crystal structure by means of X-rays," an important step in the development of X-ray crystallography. He uniquely shared a Nobel Prize with his son.

German-born British astronomer and composer. Herschel composed 24 symphonies and many concertos before taking up astronomy. In 1781, while making observations, he discovered the planet [[Uranus]], the first planet found since antiquity, and George III appointed him Court Astronomer. Using prisms and thermometers, he discovered [[Infrared|infrared]] radiation. He also discovered the moons Enceladus and Mimas of [[Saturn]], and the moons Titania and Oberon of Uranus. He also found that the Martian polar ice caps vary seasonally. He worked closely with his sister, [[Caroline Herschel]], and published catalogs of nebulae listing 2,500 objects in 1802 and 5,000 in 1820. He was the first president of the Royal Astronomical Society.

English painter, engraver, cartoonist, and satirist. Born in the [[City of London]] into a lower-middle-class family, Hogarth took up an apprenticeship with an [[Engraving|engraver]] but did not complete it. Early on he engraved coats of arms and shop bills. His works are mostly satirical caricatures, ranging from [[Realism (arts)|realistic]] portraiture to comic series he called "modern moral subjects," among them *A Harlot's Progress*, *A Rake's Progress*, and *Marriage A-la-Mode*. Widely reproduced as prints in his lifetime, they made him by far the most significant English artist of his generation. Satirical political illustrations in his style are often called "Hogarthian." Charles Lamb wrote that Hogarth's pictures are read rather than looked at.

American actor. Holden played his first starring role in the [[Boxing|boxing]] drama *Golden Boy* (1939) and became one of the biggest box-office draws of the 1950s. He gained critical recognition as the screenwriter Joe Gillis in [[Billy Wilder]]'s *Sunset Boulevard* (1950), and won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Stalag 17*. He co-starred in *Sabrina* (1954), *Picnic* (1955), and *The Bridge on the River Kwai* (1957). Later he devoted much of his life to [[Wildlife conservation|wildlife conservation]] in Africa.

27th president of the United States (1909–1913) and tenth chief justice of the United States (1921–1930), the only person to hold both offices. Born in [[Cincinnati]], Taft was appointed civilian governor of the [[Philippines]] by [[William McKinley]] and became secretary of war under [[Theodore Roosevelt]], his hand-picked successor. His administration was torn between Republican conservatives and progressives; when Roosevelt challenged him for the 1912 nomination, [[Woodrow Wilson]] won the presidency. Taft later taught at [[Yale University|Yale]], and as chief justice culminated his court administrative reform in the Judiciary Act of 1925. Historians rank him near the middle of U.S. presidents.

American actor. Trained at the [[Juilliard School]], Hurt made his film debut in *Altered States* (1980) and won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Kiss of the Spider Woman* (1985). He also received a BAFTA Award and a [[Cannes Film Festival]] Best Actor award, and was nominated for a Tony Award for his Broadway debut in *Hurlyburly*. From 2008 he played Thaddeus Ross in five films of the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]].

Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic from 1672 and king of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 1689 to 1702. Born Prince of Orange, William led resistance to the expansionism of [[Louis XIV]] and rebuilt the Dutch army after the French invasion of 1672. Backed by English leaders opposed to the policies of his uncle and father-in-law, James II, he invaded England in November 1688. James was deposed in the [[Glorious Revolution]], and William ruled jointly with his wife, Mary II, until her death in 1694. The event led to the English Bill of Rights. William's role in ordering the Massacre of Glencoe in Scotland remains notorious. Having no children, he was succeeded by Anne, Mary's sister.

King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of Hanover (1830–1837). The third son of [[George III]], William served in the [[Royal Navy]] as a young man and was nicknamed the "Sailor King." His reign saw the Reform Act 1832, the restriction of child labor, and the abolition of slavery in nearly all of the [[British Empire]]. He was the last British monarch to appoint a prime minister against the will of Parliament. With no surviving legitimate children, he was succeeded by his niece Victoria in the United Kingdom and by his brother Ernest Augustus in Hanover.

American philosopher and psychologist, often called the father of American psychology. James taught anatomy at [[Harvard University|Harvard]] and was the first educator to offer a psychology course in the United States. *The Principles of Psychology* (1890) was a groundbreaking text in the field. With [[Charles Sanders Peirce]], he established [[Pragmatism|pragmatism]], and he also developed radical empiricism. *The Varieties of Religious Experience* examined religious experience, including mysticism, from a psychological standpoint. A 1991 survey ranked him second among psychologists, after [[Wilhelm Wundt]], the founder of experimental psychology. His work influenced [[John Dewey]] and Ludwig Wittgenstein.

25th president of the United States (1897–1901). A Republican and [[American Civil War|Civil War]] veteran who rose to brevet major, McKinley championed high protective tariffs and the gold standard. He defeated William Jennings Bryan in 1896 and 1900. His presidency oversaw the [[Spanish–American War]] and the annexation of [[Hawaii]], [[Puerto Rico]], [[Guam]], and the [[Philippines]]. He was shot by an anarchist in September 1901 and succeeded by [[Theodore Roosevelt]].

British statesman and prime minister, known as Pitt the Younger to distinguish him from his father. He became prime minister at 24, the youngest in British and world history, and served eighteen years and 343 days in total, second only to [[Robert Walpole]]. He was the last prime minister of Great Britain and the first of the [[United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland|United Kingdom]]. His premiership was dominated by the [[French Revolution]] and the [[Napoleonic Wars]]; he raised taxes to fund the war against France and cracked down on radicalism at home. To counter Irish support for France, he engineered the Acts of Union 1800, but his attempt to secure Catholic emancipation as part of the Union failed. He was also Chancellor of the Exchequer throughout his premiership.

American newspaper publisher and Democratic politician, who built the largest newspaper and magazine business in the world. Born in [[San Francisco]], he took over the *San Francisco Examiner* and then bought the *New York Journal*, fighting a circulation war with [[Joseph Pulitzer]] through giant headlines and sensational stories. His chain eventually numbered nearly 30 newspapers. Twice elected to the U.S. House of Representatives as a Democrat, he ran unsuccessfully for president in 1904, and for mayor of New York City and governor of New York. His papers sensationalized Spanish atrocities in Cuba and pressed for war in 1898; he later claimed to have started the war, a claim historians reject as exaggerated. After World War I he promoted isolationism, and in the 1930s he ordered favorable coverage of [[Nazi Germany]]. Heavy debts during the Great Depression forced him to liquidate most of his assets in the late 1930s.

Irish mathematician, physicist, and astronomer. As a boy Hamilton learned about a dozen languages, and by age 16 he had covered much of Newton's *Principia*. He made major contributions to [[Algebra|algebra]], [[Classical mechanics|classical mechanics]], and [[Optics|optics]]. His invention of [[Quaternion|quaternions]], a system of four-dimensional numbers, made him one of the founders of modern [[Linear algebra|linear algebra]]. His reformulation of [[Lagrangian mechanics]] is considered fundamental to modern theoretical physics. He was Andrews Professor of Astronomy at Trinity College Dublin and director of Dunsink Observatory from 1827 until his death, and was knighted in 1835. He is regarded as arguably the most influential Irish physicist, along with Ernest Walton.

American writer and visual artist, a central figure of the Beat Generation. Born into a wealthy family in St. Louis, he attended [[Harvard University|Harvard]] and then medical school in Vienna before turning to [[Morphine|morphine]] and then heroin, an addiction that shaped much of his work. His experimental novels, including *Junkie* (1953) and *Naked Lunch* (1959), feature unreliable narrators and the cut-up technique he popularized with Brion Gysin. In 1951 he killed his second wife, Joan Vollmer, in [[Mexico City]]. [[Jack Kerouac]] called him the "greatest satirical writer since [[Jonathan Swift]]."

Canadian actor, best known for playing Captain James T. Kirk in the [[Star Trek]] franchise. From 1966 to 1994 he played Kirk across the franchise, including the original series and seven films. He also starred as attorney Denny Crane in *The Practice* and *Boston Legal*, winning two Emmy Awards. As a recording artist he is known for dramatic recitations of songs, such as versions of [[The Beatles]]' "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds." In 2021, at age 90, he became the oldest person to fly in space, on a Blue Origin suborbital flight.

American physicist and co-inventor of the [[Transistor|transistor]]. Shockley managed a research group at [[Bell Labs]] that included [[John Bardeen]] and Walter Brattain; the three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for their work on semiconductors and the transistor effect. During [[World War II]] he worked on radar research. His attempts to commercialize a new transistor design helped make [[Silicon Valley]] a hub of electronics innovation, although his autocratic management led many employees to leave and found major companies. As a professor at [[Stanford University]] in later life, he became known for his outspoken promotion of racism and [[Eugenics|eugenics]].

Scottish knight and leader in the First War of Scottish Independence. With Andrew Moray, Wallace defeated an English army at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297 and was appointed Guardian of Scotland, a post he held until his defeat at Falkirk in 1298. Captured near [[Glasgow]] in 1305, he was handed to [[Edward I]] of England, who had him hanged, drawn, and quartered for treason. Since then he has legendary status beyond [[Scotland]]: he is the protagonist of Blind Harry's 15th-century epic *The Wallace*, and the subject of the Academy Award-winning film *Braveheart*.
